Main articles: [List of presidents of the United States by other offices held](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_other_offices_held "List of presidents of the United States by other offices held"), [List of presidents of the United States by previous experience](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_previous_experience "List of presidents of the United States by previous experience"), and [List of presidents of the United States by education](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_education "List of presidents of the United States by education")

There are no requirements for previous or concurrent offices held by the president or presidential candidates. However, every president except Donald Trump has been a [governor](/wiki/Governor_(United_States) "Governor (United States)"), [U.S. senator](/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") or [Congressman](/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), [general](/wiki/General_officers_in_the_United_States "General officers in the United States") or [cabinet member](/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States").

The most common previous profession of presidents is lawyer, applying to 27 of the 45 men who have served as president.[[133]](#cite_note-139) Several future presidents abandoned the study or practice of law prior to the presidency. There has never been a property qualification for the presidency or other federal offices, but, in the early years of the republic, there were [property qualifications for voting](/wiki/Property_qualification#United_States_of_America "Property qualification") or for some of the stepping-stone offices to the presidency, particularly governorships. Prior to the Civil War, it was common for presidents to be men of significant property: Presidents from the North tended to own small farms, while several Southern presidents owned plantations and [slaves](/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_who_owned_slaves "List of presidents of the United States who owned slaves").[[134]](#cite_note-24

Populations of the African forest elephant in [Central Africa](/wiki/Central_Africa "Central Africa") range in large contiguous rainforest tracts from [Cameroon](/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon") to the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"),[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) with the largest stable population in [Gabon](/wiki/Gabon "Gabon"),[[21]](#cite_note-21) where suitable habitat covers 90% of the country.[[22]](#cite_note-abc2021-22)

They are also distributed in the evergreen moist deciduous [Upper Guinean forests](/wiki/Upper_Guinean_forest "Upper Guinean forest") in [Ivory Coast](/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast") and [Ghana](/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"), in [West Africa](/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa").[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

A group of about 10-25 African forest elephants has been sighted on the escarpment to the east of Luanda in the [Kambondo forest](/w/index.php?title=Kambondo_forest&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kambondo forest (page does not exist)") in 2015.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Nonetheless, it was estimated that the population of African forest elephants in Central Africa had declined by around 86% (in the 31 years preceding 2021) due to poaching and loss of habitat. In places such as Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, [Republic of the Congo](/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo "Republic of the Congo") and the [Central African Republic](/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic"), many areas of appropriate forest habitat have been reduced after years of warfare and human conflict.[[22]](#cite_note-abc2021-22) As of 2021, an estimated 95,000 forest elephants lived in Gabon. Prior to this the population had been estimated at 50,000 to 60,000 individuals.[[22]](#cite_note-abc2021-22)

The [Philadelphia Eagles](/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles "Philadelphia Eagles") are presented with the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy") after winning [Super Bowl LII](/wiki/Super_Bowl_LII "Super Bowl LII"), February 4, 2018.

In the AFC, this era was dominated by the Patriots, with the only four other teams to represent the conference being the Steelers, Ravens, Broncos, and Chiefs. The Patriots had tied a record with the 1970s Dallas Cowboys for most Super Bowl appearances in a decade with five appearances (2011, 2014, 2016, 2017, 2018). The Patriots also had four Super Bowl appearances in five years. They also had eight consecutive AFC championship appearances spanning 2011–2018.[[92]](#cite_note-94)

The Super Bowls of the 2000s and 2010s saw strong performances from several of the participating quarterbacks, especially on the AFC side with repeated appearances by the same teams and players. In particular, Tom Brady, [Ben Roethlisberger](/wiki/Ben_Roethlisberger "Ben Roethlisberger"), or [Peyton Manning](/wiki/Peyton_Manning "Peyton Manning") appeared as the AFC team's quarterback in all but two of the Super Bowls from 2001 through 2018.[[93]](#cite_note-95) Conversely, the only NFC teams to make the Super Bowl multiple times with the same quarterback in this era were the Seahawks, led by quarterback [Russell Wilson](/wiki/Russell_Wilson "Russell Wilson"), and the Giants, led by quarterback Eli Manning.
